3.1 Compare and contrast security implications of architecture models

A hospital's infusion pumps run a vendor-controlled real-time operating system (RTOS). The hospital can't patch them, and the vendor releases fixes only once a year. What is the best way to reduce the risk?
Place the pumps on a dedicated, segmented network with tightly restricted access and monitoring
Connect the pumps directly to the internet so the vendor can manage them
Replace their firmware with a general-purpose operating system
When devices can't be patched, compensating controls such as segmentation, strict access rules, and monitoring limit exposure.
Embedded RTOS devices usually can't run antivirus, internet exposure increases risk, and replacing medical device firmware would void its certification and support.
3.1 Compare and contrast security implications of architecture models
Compared with virtual machines, what security implication of containers must architects consider?
Containers each run a separate kernel, so they're fully isolated by hardware
Containers share the host operating system's kernel, so a kernel vulnerability or container escape can affect every container on the host
Containers can't be scanned for vulnerabilities
Containers isolate processes but share the host kernel, so the isolation boundary is weaker than a hypervisor's; hardening the host and limiting container privileges matter.
Containers are routinely image-scanned and need access controls like anything else.
3.1 Compare and contrast security implications of architecture models

A farm deploys thousands of battery-powered soil sensors that send readings every 10 minutes. The security team wants to install an EDR agent and use strong, compute-heavy encryption on each sensor. What architectural consideration makes this impractical?
The sensors' limited power and compute resources
Risk transference to the sensor vendor
Embedded and IoT devices often have constrained processors, memory, and battery life, which limits the security software and cryptography they can run.
That's why protection is usually applied at the gateway and network level, with lightweight cryptography on the device itself.
3.2 Apply security principles to secure enterprise infrastructure

An inline intrusion prevention system protects the network segment that holds cardholder data. Policy says that if the IPS fails, no traffic may pass uninspected into that segment, even if this causes an outage. How should the IPS be configured to fail?
Fail-closed blocks traffic when the device fails, putting security ahead of availability.
Fail-open would let traffic through uninspected, and passive taps or monitor-only sensors aren't inline, so they couldn't block anything even when working.
3.2 Apply security principles to secure enterprise infrastructure

Administrators may manage production database servers only by first connecting to a single hardened, closely monitored host in the management zone, and then connecting from there to the servers. What is this intermediary host?
A jump server (jump box) is a hardened, audited entry point for administering systems in a secure zone.
A forward proxy brokers outbound web traffic, a load balancer distributes requests, and an IDS sensor watches traffic.
3.2 Apply security principles to secure enterprise infrastructure

A company wants every device that plugs into a wall jack to authenticate before it gets network access. The switch should pass credentials to a RADIUS server using EAP and only open the port once authentication succeeds. What should be implemented?
802.1X makes the switch an authenticator that relays EAP credentials to a RADIUS server and grants access only after authentication succeeds.
Port mirroring copies traffic for monitoring, MAC flooding protection limits MAC addresses per port, and STP prevents switching loops.
3.2 Apply security principles to secure enterprise infrastructure

A public web application keeps getting hit with SQL injection and cross-site scripting attempts. The company wants a control in front of the application that inspects HTTP requests and blocks these application-layer attacks. What should it deploy?
A unified threat management (UTM) appliance at the branch office

A WAF inspects HTTP/HTTPS traffic at layer 7 and blocks web attacks such as SQL injection and XSS. Layer 4 firewalls and packet filters only see addresses, ports, and protocols, and a branch UTM is a general multifunction device rather than one placed in front of this application.
3.2 Apply security principles to secure enterprise infrastructure

A security team needs a perimeter firewall that can identify applications regardless of the port they use, write rules based on user identity, and include intrusion prevention, all in one device. Which firewall type fits?
An NGFW adds application awareness, user-based policy, and integrated IPS on top of stateful filtering.
A stateless filter only checks packet headers, a WAF protects web applications specifically, and a proxy brokers connections without full firewall functions.
3.2 Apply security principles to secure enterprise infrastructure
A team wants visibility into suspicious traffic on a busy trading network, but must not add latency or risk blocking legitimate trades. Which deployment fits these requirements?
An inline IPS set to fail-closed
An inline IPS set to fail-open
A passive IDS receiving a copy of the traffic from a network tap or SPAN port
A passive IDS analyzes a copy of the traffic, so it adds no latency and can't block anything; it only alerts.
Any inline device, whether an IPS or a blocking WAF, sits in the traffic path and can add latency or drop legitimate traffic.
3.2 Apply security principles to secure enterprise infrastructure

Policy requires that all traffic from remote employees' laptops, including general web browsing, pass through the company's security inspection stack while they're connected. Which VPN configuration meets this requirement?
A full tunnel sends all traffic, including internet-bound traffic, through the corporate VPN for inspection.
A split tunnel sends only corporate-bound traffic through the VPN and lets other traffic go straight to the internet. SD-WAN connects sites, and a jump server is for administration.
3.2 Apply security principles to secure enterprise infrastructure

Two offices connect over the internet with a site-to-site IPsec VPN between their gateways. The design requires that each entire original IP packet, including its internal source and destination addresses, be encrypted and given a new outer header. Which IPsec configuration provides this?
Tunnel mode with Encapsulating Security Payload (ESP)
Tunnel mode encapsulates the whole original packet inside a new IP header, and ESP provides encryption, which together hide the internal addresses between gateways.
Transport mode protects only the payload, AH authenticates but doesn't encrypt, TLS 1.0 is deprecated and isn't IPsec, and plain GRE has no encryption.
3.2 Apply security principles to secure enterprise infrastructure

A retail chain wants each store to use a mix of broadband, LTE, and MPLS links. Application traffic should be routed dynamically over the best available link, with policies managed from one central console. Which technology fits?
A forward proxy at each store
SD-WAN abstracts multiple WAN links and steers traffic by application policy from a central controller.
MPLS alone doesn't use broadband or LTE dynamically, a jump server is for administration, and proxies broker web traffic.
3.2 Apply security principles to secure enterprise infrastructure

A company with many remote workers and small branches wants secure web gateway, CASB, zero trust network access, and firewall-as-a-service delivered from cloud points of presence close to users, rather than backhauling traffic to headquarters. What architecture is this?
A unified threat management appliance at headquarters
SASE combines networking with cloud-delivered security services such as SWG, CASB, ZTNA, and FWaaS at the edge, close to users.
SD-WAN handles connectivity without the full security stack, while a headquarters UTM or site-to-site VPN requires backhauling traffic.
3.3 Compare and contrast concepts and strategies to protect data
A beverage company's flagship product depends on a secret recipe that gives it a competitive advantage and is known only to a few employees. How is this data best classified by type?
A trade secret is confidential business information that provides a competitive advantage and is protected by keeping it secret.
It isn't governed by a specific regulation, isn't public, and isn't financial information.
3.3 Compare and contrast concepts and strategies to protect data
Which data state is the hardest to protect with traditional encryption, because the data must be decrypted so the CPU can process it?
Data in use sits in memory and CPU registers in decrypted form while it's processed; technologies such as secure enclaves and confidential computing address this.
Data at rest and data in transit are routinely protected with storage encryption and TLS.
3.3 Compare and contrast concepts and strategies to protect data

A US company collects data from customers in Germany. Its legal team says the data is subject to EU law, which affects where it can be stored and who can access it, no matter where the company is headquartered. Which concept is the legal team describing?
Data sovereignty means data is subject to the laws of the country or region where it is collected or stored.
Geolocation identifies where a user or device is, masking hides parts of data, and classification labels data by sensitivity.
3.3 Compare and contrast concepts and strategies to protect data

Call center agents need to confirm a caller's identity, but their screen should show only the last four digits of the customer's Social Security number, for example `***-**-6789`. Which method is this?
Masking hides part of the data when it's displayed so users see only what they need.
Tokenization replaces the whole value with a token, hashing produces a one-way digest, and steganography hides data inside other files.
3.3 Compare and contrast concepts and strategies to protect data
Marketing produces a product brochure that will be posted on the company's public website and handed out at trade shows. Which data classification is appropriate?
Information intended for anyone to see, with no harm from disclosure, is public.
Confidential and restricted data require access controls, and critical data is essential to operations.
3.3 Compare and contrast concepts and strategies to protect data
A clinic stores patient diagnoses and treatment histories that are subject to HIPAA, which imposes specific legal requirements on how the data is protected and disclosed. What type of data is this?
Regulated data is governed by laws or regulations, such as HIPAA for health information or PCI DSS for card data, that dictate how it must be handled.
It isn't public, and it isn't a business secret or intellectual property.
3.3 Compare and contrast concepts and strategies to protect data

A company operates only in the United States and Canada. To reduce risk, it configures its cloud admin portal to reject sign-in attempts that come from IP addresses in any other country. Which data protection method is this?
Geographic restrictions limit access based on where a request appears to come from.
Hashing protects integrity, segmentation separates network zones, and obfuscation makes data harder to understand.
3.3 Compare and contrast concepts and strategies to protect data

A digital forensics team copies a suspect's hard drive. Later, in court, it must prove that the copy hasn't changed since it was acquired. Which method should it use when acquiring the image and again before presenting it?
Hashing the image at acquisition and again later shows integrity: matching hashes prove nothing changed.
Encryption protects confidentiality, while tokenization and masking hide sensitive values.
3.4 Explain the importance of resilience and recovery

A company needs a recovery site that can be operational within about a day. The site will have power, networking, and servers already in place, but data must be restored from the most recent backups before operations resume. Which site type is this?
A warm site has infrastructure and hardware ready but needs current data loaded, so recovery takes hours to days.
A hot site has live, replicated data and can take over almost immediately, while a cold site has only space and power, with equipment still to be installed.
3.4 Explain the importance of resilience and recovery
Four web servers all serve customer traffic at the same time. If one fails, the others keep handling requests and users notice nothing. Which high availability approach is this?
Load balancing spreads traffic across multiple active servers and routes around a failed one, giving both capacity and availability.
A cold standby needs time to start, and journaling and snapshots are data recovery techniques rather than live availability.
3.4 Explain the importance of resilience and recovery

The incident response and IT leaders meet in a conference room and talk through how they would respond to a scenario in which the primary data center floods. They don't touch any systems. What type of test is this?
A tabletop exercise is a discussion-based walkthrough of a scenario that tests plans and roles without affecting systems.
Failover and full interruption tests actually switch or stop systems, and parallel processing runs systems at the recovery site alongside production.
3.4 Explain the importance of resilience and recovery
Ransomware encrypts a company's production servers and every backup copy reachable over the network. Which backup practice would most reliably have allowed recovery?
Taking backups more often to the same network share
Keeping an offline or immutable copy of backups offsite
Storing the backups on the same servers as the data
Offline, air-gapped, or immutable offsite copies can't be reached or altered by ransomware moving through the network.
More frequent backups to the same share, or storing them on the same servers, would be encrypted too, and disabling encryption weakens confidentiality without helping recovery.
3.4 Explain the importance of resilience and recovery
A company's primary and backup data centers are 25 miles apart on the same coastline. A risk review notes that a single hurricane could disable both. Which resilience concept addresses this weakness?
Geographic dispersion places sites far enough apart that one regional disaster can't take out both.
Platform diversity uses different technologies to avoid a shared flaw, clustering provides local failover, and journaling records changes for data recovery.
3.4 Explain the importance of resilience and recovery
A data center has a diesel generator that takes about 45 seconds to start and stabilize after a utility power failure. What keeps the servers running without interruption during that gap?
A second generator of the same type
A UPS supplies battery power instantly when utility power fails, bridging the gap until the generator takes the load.
A second generator would have the same start-up delay, a basic PDU only distributes power, and a hot site is a separate facility.
3.4 Explain the importance of resilience and recovery
During a two-day outage, recovery stalls overnight because only one engineer knows how to restore the core database, and she's exhausted. Which resilience practice failed?
Capacity planning for people, such as cross-training and staffing for extended incidents
Capacity planning covers people as well as technology and infrastructure, so critical skills need backups and staffing must cover long incidents.
The other options deal with technology and facilities, not a single-person dependency.
3.4 Explain the importance of resilience and recovery

A faulty application update corrupts a database. Synchronous replication copies the corruption to the secondary site within seconds, so failing over doesn't help. What would have let the team return to a clean state quickly?
Point-in-time snapshots or backups taken before the update
A faster network link between sites
Replication protects against site failure, but it faithfully copies bad data too.
Point-in-time snapshots or backups let you roll back to before the corruption. More replicas, faster links, and load balancers would only spread or serve the corrupted data.
4.1 Apply common security techniques to computing resources

Before installing access points in a new warehouse, the network team walks the building with measuring tools to record signal strength and interference. It then produces a map showing coverage and dead zones. What is this activity?
A wireless site survey with heat maps
A site survey measures radio conditions and produces heat maps that guide where to place access points and how to configure power and channels.
War driving is searching for networks from outside, and pen tests and packet captures serve other purposes.
4.1 Apply common security techniques to computing resources

A company wants employees to authenticate to its Wi-Fi with their own corporate credentials through RADIUS, so access can be revoked per user, rather than everyone sharing a passphrase. Which configuration fits?
Enterprise mode uses 802.1X with RADIUS so each user authenticates individually, and WPA3 adds stronger protections.
Personal modes rely on a shared passphrase, and WEP is broken.
4.1 Apply common security techniques to computing resources
A company buys smartphones for its sales staff, keeps full ownership and management of them, and allows employees to use them for personal purposes as well. Which mobile deployment model is this?
In COPE, the organization owns and manages the device but permits personal use.
In BYOD the employee owns the device, CYOD lets employees pick from approved models (usually company-owned), and VDI delivers desktops virtually rather than being a device ownership model.
4.1 Apply common security techniques to computing resources

An executive loses a company tablet in an airport. Security needs to remotely wipe it, and it wants to require a passcode and encryption on all mobile devices going forward. Which solution provides these capabilities?
MDM enforces policies such as passcodes and encryption and can lock or wipe devices remotely.
NAC controls network admission, DLP stops sensitive data leaving, and SIEM aggregates and analyzes logs.
4.1 Apply common security techniques to computing resources
A penetration test finds that a web application's session cookie is sent over unencrypted HTTP and can be read by JavaScript running on the page. Which cookie attributes should developers set?

Secure limits the cookie to HTTPS, and HttpOnly prevents client-side scripts from reading it, which reduces theft through sniffing and XSS. Domain, Path, and expiry settings control scope and lifetime, and SameSite=None actually loosens cross-site protections.
4.1 Apply common security techniques to computing resources
A development team wants to find flaws such as hard-coded passwords and unsafe input handling by analyzing source code during the build, without running the application. What technique is this?
Static analysis (SAST) examines source or compiled code without executing it, so problems are caught early in the pipeline.
Dynamic analysis and penetration testing exercise a running application, and sandboxing runs untrusted code in isolation.
4.1 Apply common security techniques to computing resources

The email gateway receives an attachment it hasn't seen before. Before delivering it, the gateway opens the file in an isolated virtual environment and watches whether it tries to contact external servers or change system files. What technique is this?
Sandboxing runs untrusted content in an isolated environment to observe its behavior safely.
Code signing proves who published software, input validation checks data entering an application, and static analysis reviews code without running it.
4.2 Explain the security implications of hardware, software, and data asset management
A network scan finds 60 devices that don't appear in any company record, and nobody can say who is responsible for them. What should the organization establish first to manage these assets?
An accurate asset inventory with an assigned owner for each asset
You can't secure what you don't know about.

An accurate inventory with assigned ownership is the foundation for patching, monitoring, and accountability. Firewall rules, bug bounties, and retention policies don't solve the unknown-asset problem.
4.2 Explain the security implications of hardware, software, and data asset management
A hospital hires a vendor to destroy old drives that held patient records. Auditors will later want documented proof that each drive was destroyed. What should the hospital get from the vendor?
A chain of custody form for an incident
A certificate of destruction documents which media were destroyed, when, and how, providing evidence for audits.
A retention policy defines how long data is kept, chain of custody tracks evidence in investigations, and scan reports cover vulnerabilities.
4.2 Explain the security implications of hardware, software, and data asset management
A company wants to reissue laptops to new employees after previous staff leave, so the drives must be reusable, but no prior data can be recoverable. Which disposal approach fits?
Sanitization, such as cryptographic erase or secure overwrite
Deleting files and emptying the recycle bin
Reformatting the drive with a quick format
Sanitization makes data unrecoverable while keeping the media usable.
Shredding destroys the drive, and deleting files or quick formatting leaves recoverable data.
4.2 Explain the security implications of hardware, software, and data asset management
Regulations require a company to keep financial transaction records for seven years and then securely delete them. Which policy governs this?
A data retention policy defines how long each type of data is kept and how it's disposed of afterward.
The other policies cover acceptable behavior, changes to systems, and responding to incidents.
4.2 Explain the security implications of hardware, software, and data asset management

A company keeps buying network cameras that later turn out to lack firmware updates and encryption. At what stage of the asset lifecycle is it best to make sure new devices meet security requirements?
During acquisition and procurement, by including security requirements before purchase
Building security requirements into procurement prevents insecure assets from entering the environment, which is cheaper than fixing them afterward.
Disposal, incidents, and audits all come too late to influence what was bought.
4.3 Explain activities associated with vulnerability management

A scan reports two findings: a CVSS 9.8 vulnerability on an isolated lab server with no network connectivity and no sensitive data, and a CVSS 6.5 vulnerability on an internet-facing server that processes card payments. Which should normally be fixed first, and why?
The 9.8 finding, because the highest CVSS base score always comes first
Neither; both should be accepted as risks
The 6.5 finding, because exposure and environmental factors make it the greater real risk to the business
The 9.8 finding, because lab systems are the most valuable
Prioritization should weigh exposure, asset value, and environmental variables, not just the base score.
An internet-facing payment system with a known flaw is more likely to be exploited and more damaging. Base scores alone can mislead, and accepting both risks ignores real exposure.
4.3 Explain activities associated with vulnerability management

A vulnerability scanner flags a critical Apache flaw based on the version string in the server banner. On investigation, the analyst confirms the vendor backported the fix into that package, so the server isn't actually vulnerable. What is the scan finding?
A false positive reports a vulnerability that doesn't actually exist; confirmation is part of vulnerability analysis.
A false negative misses a real vulnerability, a true positive is a correct finding, and a zero-day has no available fix.
4.3 Explain activities associated with vulnerability management
Scans of Windows servers show very few missing patches, but a manual check finds many. The scanner was only probing network services from outside. What change would make the results more accurate?
Running credentialed (authenticated) scans so the scanner can inspect installed software and configuration
Switching to a passive network sniffer
Credentialed scans log in to the system and see installed packages, patches, and settings, which greatly reduces false negatives.
Less frequent scans, external-only scans, and passive sniffing all provide less visibility.
4.3 Explain activities associated with vulnerability management
A software company publishes rules that let outside researchers test its products, explains how to report findings safely, and pays rewards based on severity. What is this program?
A bug bounty program invites outside researchers to find and responsibly disclose vulnerabilities in exchange for rewards.
A penetration test is a contracted, scoped engagement, threat feeds share information about threats, and audits check compliance.
4.3 Explain activities associated with vulnerability management

A critical patch for a laboratory instrument controller can't be installed for 60 days, because the vendor must first certify it. The security team documents the risk, gets the business owner's approval, isolates the controller on a restricted segment, and sets a review date. What is this remediation approach?
A formal exception with compensating controls
An exception (or exemption) formally accepts a vulnerability for a defined period with documented approval, compensating controls, and a review date.
Insurance transfers financial impact, rescanning verifies fixes, and ignoring the vulnerability has no approval or controls.
4.3 Explain activities associated with vulnerability management
An administrator reports that all servers affected by a critical OpenSSL vulnerability have been patched. Before closing the ticket, what should the security team do to validate the remediation?
Close the ticket based on the administrator's report
Subscribe to a new threat feed
Rescan the affected systems to verify the vulnerability is gone
Validation confirms remediation actually worked, typically by rescanning or verifying configuration.
Taking someone's word for it skips validation, and threat feeds and bug bounties are about finding vulnerabilities, not confirming fixes.
4.3 Explain activities associated with vulnerability management
After applying all reasonable controls, the board decides to buy cyber insurance to cover the remaining financial impact of a possible ransomware attack. Which response does this represent?
Insurance transfers the financial consequences of a risk to another party, though it doesn't stop the attack itself.
Avoidance means stopping the risky activity, segmentation reduces likelihood or impact, and an exception temporarily accepts a specific vulnerability.
4.4 Explain security alerting and monitoring concepts and tools

A security team wants to collect logs from firewalls, servers, the identity provider, and endpoints in one place. It needs to correlate events across them, for example many failed logins followed by a success from a new country, and raise alerts. Which tool fits?
A SIEM aggregates and normalizes logs from many sources, correlates events, and generates alerts and reports.
SNMP monitors device status, NetFlow records traffic flows, and antivirus protects individual endpoints.
4.4 Explain security alerting and monitoring concepts and tools
The SOC receives hundreds of alerts every night from a legitimate backup job that a rule flags as "mass file access." Analysts have started ignoring the queue. What should the team do?
Tune the alert, for example by excluding the known backup account or adjusting thresholds
Alert tuning reduces false positives so real alerts get attention, which addresses alert fatigue.
Archiving doesn't reduce noise, quarantining a legitimate server disrupts operations, and disabling aggregation removes visibility.
4.4 Explain security alerting and monitoring concepts and tools

An auditor asks for proof that 500 Linux and Windows servers are configured according to CIS Benchmarks. The team needs automated, standardized checks that produce a compliance report. What should it use?
Manual spot checks of ten servers
A packet capture of server traffic
A SCAP-compliant scanner with CIS Benchmark content

SCAP (Security Content Automation Protocol) standardizes how configuration checks are expressed and evaluated, so tools can automatically assess systems against benchmarks such as CIS. Spot checks don't scale, and NetFlow and packet captures show traffic, not configuration.
4.4 Explain security alerting and monitoring concepts and tools
An analyst needs to see which internal hosts talked to which external IP addresses, when, and how much data moved, without storing the full contents of every packet. Which data source fits?
NetFlow records flow metadata (source, destination, ports, timing, and volume) without payloads, which is efficient for spotting exfiltration and unusual connections.
Packet capture stores full contents, SNMP traps report device events, and debug logs cover one application.
4.4 Explain security alerting and monitoring concepts and tools
A company wants to detect and block emails and uploads that contain customer credit card numbers or files labeled "Confidential" before they leave the organization. Which tool fits?
DLP inspects content leaving through email, web, or endpoints and blocks or alerts on sensitive data.
EDR focuses on endpoint threats, NAC controls network admission, and a WAF protects web applications from incoming attacks.
4.4 Explain security alerting and monitoring concepts and tools
The team wants to monitor printers, storage appliances, and network switches, which can't run third-party software. Which monitoring approach fits these devices?
Agentless monitoring using protocols and APIs such as SNMP, syslog, or vendor APIs
Installing an EDR agent on each device
No monitoring, since appliances are secure by default
Agentless monitoring collects data remotely when software can't be installed.
EDR and antivirus agents need an installable operating system, and appliances still need monitoring.
4.5 Modify enterprise capabilities to enhance security

An administrator adds a rule allowing HTTPS to the new web server, but connections still fail. The rule list shows "Deny any any" as rule 3 and the new allow rule as rule 9. What is the likely cause and fix?
HTTPS needs port 80 opened as well
The server needs a new IP address
Firewalls process rules bottom-up, so the deny rule should be moved down
Rules are processed top-down, so the deny rule matches first; place the allow rule above the deny rule
Firewalls generally evaluate rules from top to bottom and apply the first match, so a broad deny placed earlier blocks traffic that later rules would allow.
Specific allow rules go above the default deny, which belongs at the end. HTTPS uses port 443, and the IP address isn't the issue.
4.5 Modify enterprise capabilities to enhance security

A company is publishing a public-facing web server and wants it isolated from the internal network, so that a compromise of the web server doesn't give direct access to internal systems. Where should the server go?
In a screened subnet (DMZ) between the external and internal firewalls
Directly on the internet with no firewall
On the same segment as the domain controllers
A screened subnet hosts public services in a separate zone with firewall rules controlling traffic to the internet and to the internal network.
The internal VLAN and the domain controller segment expose internal systems, and having no firewall leaves the server unprotected.
4.5 Modify enterprise capabilities to enhance security

A company wants to stop all devices on its network, including IoT devices and guest laptops that can't run agents, from reaching known malware and phishing domains. Which control works without installing anything on the devices?
DNS filtering at the organization's resolvers
DNS filtering blocks lookups of malicious domains for every device that uses the organization's resolvers, with no agent needed.
Agent-based filters need software on each device, a WAF protects web applications, and DLP focuses on data leaving.
4.5 Modify enterprise capabilities to enhance security

Attackers are sending phishing emails that appear to come from @example.com through servers the company doesn't control. Which DNS record lets receiving mail servers check whether the sending server is authorized to send mail for the domain?
DMARC (Domain-based Message Authentication, Reporting, and Conformance)
SPF publishes the list of servers authorized to send for a domain.
DKIM signs messages to prove they weren't altered, DMARC sets the policy for failures and enables reporting, and S/MIME signs or encrypts individual messages for end users.
4.5 Modify enterprise capabilities to enhance security

A company already publishes SPF and signs outgoing mail with DKIM. It now wants receiving servers to reject messages claiming to be from its domain that fail those checks, and it wants reports on who is sending mail as its domain. What should it add?
A DMARC record with a policy of p=reject and reporting addresses
DMARC tells receivers what to do when SPF and DKIM checks fail or don't align with the From domain (none, quarantine, or reject) and sends aggregate reports back.
A second SPF record is invalid, a longer key doesn't create a policy, and MX records route inbound mail.
4.5 Modify enterprise capabilities to enhance security

A security team wants an alert whenever critical operating system binaries or the files in the web server's document root are modified, because attackers often plant web shells or tamper with system files. What should be deployed?
FIM compares files against known-good hashes and alerts on unauthorized changes.
Content filters control browsing, NAC controls network admission, and UBA analyzes user activity patterns.
4.5 Modify enterprise capabilities to enhance security
In a Windows Active Directory environment, an administrator needs to enforce a minimum password length and disable USB storage on all workstations from one central place. Which tool fits?
Group Policy Objects apply security settings centrally to Windows computers and users in a domain.
SELinux provides mandatory access control on Linux, a web filter controls browsing, and NAC controls network admission.
4.5 Modify enterprise capabilities to enhance security
A school district wants to block student devices from reaching gambling, adult, and known-malware sites without maintaining its own list of every URL. Which web filtering capability fits?
Content categorization with category-based block rules
A manually maintained list of URLs
Content categorization uses vendor-maintained classifications and reputation data so whole categories can be blocked at once.
Manual lists can't keep up, DMARC is email authentication, and FIM watches file changes.
4.6 Implement and maintain identity and access management

Employees sign in once to the corporate identity provider and are then logged in to several SaaS applications. The identity provider sends each application a signed XML assertion stating who the user is. Which standard is this?
SAML provides federated single sign-on using signed XML assertions from an identity provider to service providers.
LDAP is a directory protocol, Kerberos is ticket-based authentication within a domain, and RADIUS handles network access authentication.
4.6 Implement and maintain identity and access management

A scheduling app asks a user for permission to read their calendar in a cloud email service. The user approves on the provider's own page, and the app receives a limited access token without ever seeing the user's password. Which framework is this?
OAuth provides delegated authorization: an app gets a scoped token to act on the user's behalf without receiving their credentials.
SAML focuses on federated authentication for single sign-on, while LDAP and Kerberos are directory and domain authentication protocols.
4.6 Implement and maintain identity and access management

An audit finds that employees who left months ago still have active accounts in several SaaS applications, because IT disables accounts only in the main directory and only when it remembers. What should be implemented?
Automated deprovisioning triggered by HR termination events across all connected systems
Deprovisioning removes access promptly when people leave, and automating it from HR events across connected systems prevents orphaned accounts.
Password settings, scans, and firewall rules don't remove leftover access.
4.6 Implement and maintain identity and access management

A bank's policy allows access to loan files only when the user is in the Lending department, the device is company-managed, the request comes during business hours, and the file's classification is no higher than the user's clearance. Which access control model evaluates rules like these?
ABAC makes decisions by evaluating attributes of the user, resource, device, and environment, such as time of day, together.
RBAC grants access by role alone, DAC lets owners decide, and MAC relies on system-enforced labels and clearances without the device and time conditions.
4.6 Implement and maintain identity and access management

In a defense agency's system, every document is labeled Confidential, Secret, or Top Secret, and every user has a clearance level. Users can't change a document's label or share it with someone who lacks the clearance, even if they created the document. Which model is this?
In MAC, the system enforces access based on classification labels and clearances, and users can't override it.
In DAC, owners control access, RBAC grants access by job role, and rule-based control applies rules such as firewall ACLs or time windows.
4.6 Implement and maintain identity and access management
On a team file share, the person who creates a folder decides who else can read or edit it and can grant access to any colleague. Which access control model is this?
In DAC, the owner of a resource decides who gets access.
MAC is enforced by labels the owner can't change, ABAC evaluates attributes, and rule-based control applies centrally defined rules.
4.6 Implement and maintain identity and access management
Which combination is true multifactor authentication?
A password and a hardware security key
A fingerprint and a face scan
A password and the answer to a security question
MFA requires factors from different categories; a password (something you know) plus a hardware key (something you have) qualifies.
A password with a PIN or a security question uses only "something you know," and two biometrics are both "something you are."
4.6 Implement and maintain identity and access management

Domain administrators currently know the passwords of powerful accounts and use them whenever they like. The company wants admins to check out credentials from a vault only for approved tasks, have the passwords rotated automatically afterward, and have sessions recorded. Which solution fits?
Privileged access management (PAM) with password vaulting and just-in-time access
PAM tools vault privileged credentials, grant just-in-time or ephemeral access, rotate secrets, and record sessions.
SSO and federation simplify regular sign-ins, and a personal password manager doesn't provide approval workflows or session recording.
4.7 Explain the importance of automation and orchestration

When HR marks a new hire as "starting Monday," a workflow automatically creates their accounts, adds them to the right groups for their department, and assigns a laptop. Which automation use case is this?
Security group enforcement in the cloud

Automated user provisioning creates accounts and permissions consistently from an authoritative source such as HR. Continuous integration tests code, escalation routes tickets, and security groups control network access to cloud resources.
4.7 Explain the importance of automation and orchestration

When the EDR raises a high-confidence ransomware alert at 3:00 a.m., a SOAR playbook immediately isolates the laptop, disables the user's sessions, opens a ticket, and pages the on-call analyst. What is the primary benefit of this automation?
Faster reaction time, with automation acting as a workforce multiplier
Removing the need for any human analysts
Automation responds in seconds and handles repetitive steps, letting a small team cover more incidents.
Humans are still needed for judgment, automation tools carry their own costs, and automation doesn't remove false positives; tuning does that.
4.7 Explain the importance of automation and orchestration

An engineer writes one large, undocumented script that provisions every account, firewall rule, and server in the company. Then the engineer leaves. Which automation consideration does this situation illustrate most?
Complexity, technical debt, a single point of failure, and ongoing supportability
Automation brings its own risks: complex, undocumented tooling creates technical debt and a single point of failure that nobody else can support.
The other options are benefits of automation, not risks.
4.7 Explain the importance of automation and orchestration

A cloud platform team adds an automated policy check to the deployment pipeline. It blocks any storage bucket configured for public access and any VM with an open SSH port to the internet before they're created. What is this automation called?
Guardrails are automated controls that stop insecure configurations before they're deployed while still letting teams move fast.
Ticket creation and escalation handle workflow, and continuous integration builds and tests code.

Two weeks after a phishing-driven incident is resolved, the response team meets with IT and HR to review what happened, what worked, and what to change in email filtering and training. Which phase of incident response is this?
Lessons learned reviews the incident afterward to improve controls and processes.
Recovery restores operations, containment limits the spread, and preparation happens before incidents. Improvements from lessons learned do feed back into preparation.
After isolating compromised servers, responders delete the attacker's web shells, remove the accounts the attacker created, and patch the vulnerability that was exploited. Which phase is this?
Eradication removes the threat and its root cause from the environment.
Detection identifies the incident, recovery returns systems to normal operation and monitors them, and lessons learned comes last.
Which sequence correctly lists the incident response phases in the order used by CompTIA?
Preparation, detection, analysis, containment, eradication, recovery, lessons learned
Detection, preparation, eradication, containment, analysis, recovery, lessons learned
Preparation, containment, detection, analysis, recovery, eradication, lessons learned
Analysis, detection, preparation, recovery, containment, eradication, lessons learned
You prepare, detect and analyze the incident, contain it, eradicate the threat, recover systems, and then capture lessons learned.
The other orders put containment before detection or recovery before eradication, which doesn't work in practice.

A forensic analyst collects a laptop believed to have been used in fraud. She records every person who handles it, when, and why, from the moment of seizure until it's presented in court. What is this documentation?
Chain of custody documents evidence handling so its integrity can be defended in court.
A legal hold preserves data for litigation, e-discovery is the process of finding and producing electronic evidence, and RCA identifies why an incident happened.

The legal department learns that a former employee is likely to sue. It instructs IT to suspend automatic deletion of that employee's email and files and to preserve all related records. What is this instruction called?
A legal hold requires preserving relevant data when litigation is reasonably expected, overriding normal deletion schedules.
A retention policy sets normal timelines, chain of custody tracks evidence handling, and decommissioning retires assets.

With no alert having fired, an analyst forms a hypothesis that attackers might be using PowerShell to download tools. She searches endpoint telemetry across the company for encoded PowerShell commands that make network connections. What is this activity?
Threat hunting proactively searches for threats that existing tools haven't detected, often starting from a hypothesis based on attacker techniques.
Vulnerability scanning finds weaknesses, alert tuning adjusts detections, and tabletop exercises rehearse response plans.

After a breach through an unpatched VPN appliance, investigators find the patch had been released months earlier. Nobody applied it because the appliance wasn't in the asset inventory used for patching. Identifying this underlying process gap is an example of what?
Root cause analysis looks past the immediate technical cause (the missing patch) to the underlying reason (the incomplete inventory), so the fix prevents recurrence.
Containment limits damage, e-discovery produces evidence for legal matters, and threat hunting searches for active threats.
4.9 Use data sources to support an investigation
An investigator needs to confirm whether opening a malicious Word document on a laptop caused PowerShell to launch and download a file. Which data source most directly shows this process activity?
Endpoint and operating system security logs, such as EDR telemetry
Endpoint and OS logs record process creation, including which parent process launched which child, so they can show Word starting PowerShell.
Firewall and load balancer logs see network connections but not processes, and scan reports show weaknesses rather than activity.
4.9 Use data sources to support an investigation

Investigators know a compromised server made an unusual outbound connection. To determine exactly what data was sent, they need the contents of the transmitted traffic, not just its source, destination, and size. Which data source is required?
A packet capture of the traffic
Packet captures contain full payloads, which shows what was transmitted if the traffic wasn't encrypted or can be decrypted.
NetFlow and firewall logs record metadata about connections, and SNMP traps report device events.
4.9 Use data sources to support an investigation
An analyst investigating a suspicious invoice email needs to know which mail servers actually relayed it and whether it passed SPF, DKIM, and DMARC checks. Where will this information be?
A packet capture from the analyst's own workstation
The email's metadata in its message headers
Email headers are metadata recording the relay path and authentication results.
A local packet capture wouldn't show the earlier relays, firewall logs show connections without message-level details, and scanners don't analyze email.
4.9 Use data sources to support an investigation

After a web server is compromised through a known exploit, leadership asks whether the vulnerability had been detected before the attack and how long it had gone unremediated. Which data source answers this most directly?
Historical vulnerability scan reports for that server
Packet captures from the day of the attack
Past scan reports show when the vulnerability first appeared and whether it stayed open, which supports the investigation and root cause analysis.
A current dashboard, attack-day captures, and CPU graphs don't show the vulnerability's history.
5.1 Summarize elements of effective security governance

A company document states: "All company laptops must use full-disk encryption with AES-256, and recovery keys must be escrowed in the central key management system." What type of governance document is this?
A standard sets specific, mandatory requirements, such as an algorithm and key length, that support a broader policy.
A policy states high-level intent (for example, "sensitive data must be protected"), a procedure gives step-by-step instructions, and a guideline is a recommendation.
5.1 Summarize elements of effective security governance

The IT team follows a numbered checklist for every new hire: create the directory account, assign groups by role, enroll MFA, issue a laptop, and confirm completion in the ticket. What type of document is this?
A procedure gives the step-by-step instructions for carrying out a task consistently, such as onboarding.
Policies set intent, guidelines recommend, and standards define specific mandatory requirements.
5.1 Summarize elements of effective security governance
The vice president of sales is accountable for the customer CRM data. She decides its classification and approves who may access it. Which data role does she hold?
The data owner is the senior person accountable for a data set, including its classification and access approvals.
Custodians implement the technical protections, processors handle data on another organization's behalf, and data subjects are the people the data describes.
5.1 Summarize elements of effective security governance
Database administrators run nightly backups, apply the access permissions the data owner has approved, and maintain encryption on the CRM database. Which role are they performing?
Custodians, or stewards, handle the day-to-day care of data, carrying out protections as the owner directs.
The owner sets classification and access, the controller decides the purposes of processing personal data under privacy law, and the subject is the person the data is about.
5.1 Summarize elements of effective security governance

A company hires a payroll service to calculate and pay employee salaries. Under GDPR-style privacy law, the company decides what employee data is used and why, and the payroll service handles the data only on the company's instructions. What is the payroll service's role?
A processor handles personal data on behalf of, and as instructed by, the controller; here the company is the controller.
The payroll service doesn't decide the purposes of processing, isn't the internal accountable owner, and isn't the person the data describes.
5.1 Summarize elements of effective security governance

The security team publishes a document suggesting that employees use a passphrase of four or more random words. It explains this is recommended practice but not a mandatory rule. What type of document is this?
Guidelines are recommendations that help people follow policies and standards but aren't mandatory.
Standards and policies are required, and procedures are step-by-step instructions.
5.1 Summarize elements of effective security governance

In a global conglomerate, each regional business unit writes and enforces its own security policies, with little central oversight. The result is inconsistent controls across regions. Which governance structure does this describe?
Decentralized governance distributes decision-making to business units, which gives flexibility but often produces inconsistency.
Centralized governance sets common policy from one authority. A board and a government entity are governing bodies, not this distribution model.
5.2 Explain elements of the risk management process
A server's asset value is $200,000. A flood would destroy 25% of its value (the exposure factor). What is the single loss expectancy (SLE)?
The other figures misapply the formula: $800,000 multiplies instead of taking a percentage, and $200,000 ignores the exposure factor.
5.2 Explain elements of the risk management process
The same flood has a single loss expectancy of $50,000 and is expected to happen once every two years, so the annualized rate of occurrence (ARO) is 0.5. What is the annualized loss expectancy (ALE)?
ALE helps decide whether a control is worth its annual cost; for example, a $40,000-per-year control wouldn't be justified on this risk alone.
5.2 Explain elements of the risk management process
A risk committee rates each risk as High, Medium, or Low for likelihood and impact and plots them on a heat map, without assigning dollar values. What type of risk analysis is this?
Qualitative analysis uses descriptive ratings and relative rankings.
Quantitative analysis assigns numbers such as SLE, ARO, and ALE, and exposure factor is one input to those calculations.
5.2 Explain elements of the risk management process
A CISO wants one central record of all identified risks, showing each risk's owner, likelihood, impact, chosen treatment, key risk indicators, and current status. What is this document?
A risk register tracks identified risks with owners, ratings, treatments, indicators, and status over time.
A BIA determines how critical business functions are and their recovery targets, an SLA defines service commitments, and an MOU records an informal agreement between parties.
5.2 Explain elements of the risk management process
A startup's board states that it's willing to take significant risks, such as launching products quickly with fewer controls, to capture market share. Which risk appetite does this describe?
An expansionary risk appetite accepts higher risk to pursue growth.
A conservative appetite minimizes risk, a neutral one balances the two, and avoidance is a treatment for a specific risk rather than an appetite.
5.2 Explain elements of the risk management process
After assessing the legal and security risks of storing customers' biometric data, a company decides to discontinue the fingerprint login feature entirely. Which risk management strategy is this?
Avoidance eliminates a risk by stopping the activity that creates it.
Transfer shifts the impact to another party, acceptance keeps the risk as it is, and mitigation reduces it with controls.
5.2 Explain elements of the risk management process
A business impact analysis concludes that the online ordering system must be back in service within four hours of an outage, or the company will suffer unacceptable losses. Which metric is this?
RTO is the maximum acceptable time to restore a service after disruption.
RPO is the maximum acceptable data loss measured in time, MTBF is the average operating time between failures, and MTTR is the average time to repair.
5.2 Explain elements of the risk management process
The finance team says that if the trading database fails, it can afford to lose no more than 15 minutes of transactions. Which metric does this define, and how does it shape the backup design?
RTO; servers must restart within 15 minutes
MTTR; repairs must take 15 minutes on average
RPO; backups or replication must capture data at least every 15 minutes
MTBF; the database may fail only every 15 minutes
RPO sets how much data loss is acceptable, which determines backup or replication frequency.
RTO is about restoration time, MTTR is average repair time, and MTBF measures reliability between failures.
